===== .buildkite/pipeline.qodana.yml =====
# Qodana code quality pipeline — replaces .github/workflows/qodana_code_quality.yml
# Triggered on pushes to main/releases/* and on pull requests.
# Skips documentation-only changes (CHANGELOG.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, README.md, img/**).

steps:
  - label: ":qodana: Qodana Scan"
    key: qodana
    agents:
      queue: default
    env:
      QODANA_TOKEN: $${QODANA_TOKEN?}
      QODANA_ENDPOINT: "https://qodana.cloud"
    commands:
      - |
        # Skip if all changed files are documentation-only
        CHANGED="$$(git diff --name-only HEAD~1 HEAD 2>/dev/null || git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD)"
        NON_DOC="$$(echo "$$CHANGED" | grep -vE '^(CHANGELOG|CONTRIBUTING|CODE_OF_CONDUCT|README)\.md$$' | grep -v '^img/')"
        if [ -z "$$NON_DOC" ]; then
          echo "Only documentation changes detected — skipping Qodana scan."
          exit 0
        fi
      - |
        # Run Qodana via Docker (mirrors the JetBrains/qodana-action behavior)
        docker run --rm \
          -v "$$(pwd):/data/project" \
          -e QODANA_TOKEN="$$QODANA_TOKEN" \
          -e QODANA_ENDPOINT="$$QODANA_ENDPOINT" \
          jetbrains/qodana-jvm:2025.3 \
          --save-report \
          --results-dir /data/project/build/qodana/results \
          --report-dir /data/project/build/qodana/report
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/qodana/report/**/*"

# Release pipeline — replaces .github/workflows/release.yml

steps:
  - label: ":rocket: Publish Plugin"
    key: publish
    env:
      PUBLISH_TOKEN: $${PUBLISH_TOKEN?}
      CERTIFICATE_CHAIN: $${CERTIFICATE_CHAIN?}
      PRIVATE_KEY: $${PRIVATE_KEY?}
      PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD: $${PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD?}
      GITHUB_TOKEN: $${GITHUB_TOKEN?}
    plugins:
      - docker#v5.12.0:
          image: "gradle:8-jdk21"
          environment:
            - PUBLISH_TOKEN
            - CERTIFICATE_CHAIN
            - PRIVATE_KEY
            - PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD
    commands:
      - |
        TAG="$$BUILDKITE_TAG"

        if [ -z "$$RELEASE_BODY" ]; then
          RELEASE_BODY="$$(gh release view "$$TAG" --json body -q '.body')"
        fi

        CHANGELOG="$$(echo "$$RELEASE_BODY" | sed -e 's/^[[:space:]]*$$//g' -e '/./,$$!d')"

        if [ -n "$$CHANGELOG" ]; then
          gradle patchChangelog --release-note="$$CHANGELOG"
        fi

        gradle publishPlugin

        gh release upload "$$TAG" ./build/distributions/*

        if [ -n "$$CHANGELOG" ]; then
          BRANCH="changelog-update-$$TAG"

          git config user.email "buildkite@ci"
          git config user.name "Buildkite"
          git checkout -b "$$BRANCH"
          git commit -am "Changelog update - $$TAG"
          git push --set-upstream origin "$$BRANCH"

          gh label create "release changelog" \
            --description "Pull requests with release changelog update" \
            --force || true

          gh pr create \
            --title "Changelog update - \`$$TAG\`" \
            --body "Current pull request contains patched \`CHANGELOG.md\` file for the \`$$TAG\` version." \
            --label "release changelog" \
            --head "$$BRANCH"
        fi

    artifact_paths:
      - "build/distributions/*.zip"

# UI test pipeline — replaces .github/workflows/run-ui-tests.yml
# Triggered manually via `buildkite-agent pipeline upload .buildkite/pipeline.ui-tests.yml`
# or by triggering the pipeline from the Buildkite UI.

steps:
  # ─── Linux ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - label: ":linux: UI Tests (Linux)"
    key: ui-test-linux
    agents:
      os: linux
      queue: default
    env:
      JAVA_HOME: /usr/lib/jvm/zulu-21-amd64
      DISPLAY: ":99.0"
    commands:
      - Xvfb -ac :99 -screen 0 1920x1080x16 &
      - ./gradlew runIdeForUiTests &
      - |
        # Wait for IDE to be ready (equivalent to url-health-check-action)
        for i in $$(seq 1 15); do
          if curl -sf http://127.0.0.1:8082 > /dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "IDE is ready"
            break
          fi
          echo "Attempt $$i/15 — waiting 30s..."
          sleep 30
        done
      - ./gradlew test
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/reports/tests/**/*"

  # ─── macOS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - label: ":mac: UI Tests (macOS)"
    key: ui-test-macos
    agents:
      os: macos
      queue: default
    env:
      JAVA_HOME: /Library/Java/JavaVirtualMachines/zulu-21.jdk/Contents/Home
    commands:
      - ./gradlew runIdeForUiTests &
      - |
        for i in $$(seq 1 15); do
          if curl -sf http://127.0.0.1:8082 > /dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "IDE is ready"
            break
          fi
          echo "Attempt $$i/15 — waiting 30s..."
          sleep 30
        done
      - ./gradlew test
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/reports/tests/**/*"

  # ─── Windows ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  - label: ":windows: UI Tests (Windows)"
    key: ui-test-windows
    agents:
      os: windows
      queue: default
    env:
      JAVA_HOME: "C:\\Program Files\\Zulu\\zulu-21"
    commands:
      - start gradlew.bat runIdeForUiTests
      - |
        for /L %%i in (1,1,15) do (
          curl -sf http://127.0.0.1:8082 >nul 2>&1 && (echo IDE is ready & goto :ready)
          echo Attempt %%i/15 - waiting 30s...
          timeout /t 30 /nobreak >nul
        )
        :ready
      - gradlew.bat test
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/reports/tests/**/*"

# Main CI pipeline — replaces .github/workflows/build.yml

steps:
  - label: ":test_tube: Test"
    key: test
    command: "gradle check"
    plugins:
      - docker#v5.12.0:
          image: "gradle:9-jdk21"
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/reports/tests/**/*"
      - "build/reports/kover/report.xml"

  - label: ":hammer: Build"
    key: build
    # buildSearchableOptions launches a full IntelliJ IDE process and requires ~4GB RAM.
    # Skip it in CI; it only generates marketplace search indexes.
    command: "gradle buildPlugin -x buildSearchableOptions"
    plugins:
      - docker#v5.12.0:
          image: "gradle:9-jdk21"
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/distributions/*.zip"

  - label: ":shield: Verify Plugin"/
    key: verify
    command: "gradle verifyPlugin -x buildSearchableOptions --no-daemon --max-workers 1"
    plugins:
      - docker#v5.12.0:
          image: "gradle:9-jdk21"
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/reports/pluginVerifier/**/*"

  - wait: ~

  - label: ":github: Create Release Draft"
    key: release-draft
    branches: "main"
    agents:
      queue: default
    env:
      GITHUB_TOKEN: $${GITHUB_TOKEN?}
    commands:
      - |
        PROPERTIES="$$(gradle properties --console=plain -q)"
        VERSION="$$(echo "$$PROPERTIES" | grep "^version:" | cut -f2- -d ' ')"
        CHANGELOG="$$(gradle getChangelog --unreleased --no-header --console=plain -q)"

        gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases \
          --jq '.[] | select(.draft == true) | .id' \
          | xargs -I '{}' gh api -X DELETE repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases/{}

        gh release create "v$$VERSION" \
          --draft \
          --title "v$$VERSION" \
          --notes "$$CHANGELOG"

=== release.yml ===
# GitHub Actions Workflow created for handling the release process based on the draft release prepared with the Build workflow.
# Running the publishPlugin task requires all following secrets to be provided: PUBLISH_TOKEN, PRIVATE_KEY, PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD, CERTIFICATE_CHAIN.
# See https://plugins.jetbrains.com/docs/intellij/plugin-signing.html for more information.

name: Release
on:
  release:
    types: [prereleased, released]

jobs:

  # Prepare and publish the plugin to JetBrains Marketplace repository
  release:
    name: Publish Plugin
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: write
    steps:

      # Check out the current repository
      - name: Fetch Sources
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.release.tag_name }}

      # Set up Java environment for the next steps
      - name: Setup Java
        uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: zulu
          java-version: 21

      # Setup Gradle
      - name: Setup Gradle
        uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v4

      # Set environment variables
      - name: Export Properties
        id: properties
        shell: bash
        run: |
          CHANGELOG="$(cat << 'EOM' | sed -e 's/^[[:space:]]*$//g' -e '/./,$!d'
          ${{ github.event.release.body }}
          EOM
          )"
          
          echo "changelog<<EOF" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
          echo "$CHANGELOG" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
          echo "EOF" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT

      # Update the Unreleased section with the current release note
      - name: Patch Changelog
        if: ${{ steps.properties.outputs.changelog != '' }}
        env:
          CHANGELOG: ${{ steps.properties.outputs.changelog }}
        run: |
          ./gradlew patchChangelog --release-note="$CHANGELOG"

      # Publish the plugin to JetBrains Marketplace
      - name: Publish Plugin
        env:
          PUBLISH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PUBLISH_TOKEN }}
          CERTIFICATE_CHAIN: ${{ secrets.CERTIFICATE_CHAIN }}
          PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.PRIVATE_KEY }}
          PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD }}
        run: ./gradlew publishPlugin

      # Upload artifact as a release asset
      - name: Upload Release Asset
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: gh release upload ${{ github.event.release.tag_name }} ./build/distributions/*

      # Create a pull request
      - name: Create Pull Request
        if: ${{ steps.properties.outputs.changelog != '' }}
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          VERSION="${{ github.event.release.tag_name }}"
          BRANCH="changelog-update-$VERSION"
          LABEL="release changelog"

          git config user.email "action@github.com"
          git config user.name "GitHub Action"

          git checkout -b $BRANCH
          git commit -am "Changelog update - $VERSION"
          git push --set-upstream origin $BRANCH
          
          gh label create "$LABEL" \
            --description "Pull requests with release changelog update" \
            --force \
            || true

          gh pr create \
            --title "Changelog update - \`$VERSION\`" \
            --body "Current pull request contains patched \`CHANGELOG.md\` file for the \`$VERSION\` version." \
            --label "$LABEL" \
            --head $BRANCH

name: Run UI Tests

jobs:

    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:

              export DISPLAY=:99.0

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/sabufung/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/5.0.7/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Visual questions ahead?" [shape=diamond];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Visual questions ahead?";
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [label="yes"];
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Ask clarifying questions" [label="no"];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion:** When you anticipate that upcoming questions will involve visual content (mockups, layouts, diagrams), offer it once for consent:
> "Some of what we're working on might be easier to explain if I can show it to you in a web browser. I can put together mockups, diagrams, comparisons, and other visuals as we go. This feature is still new and can be token-intensive. Want to try it? (Requires opening a local URL)"

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Do not combine it with clarifying questions, context summaries, or any other content. The message should contain ONLY the offer above and nothing else. Wait for the user's response before continuing. If they decline, proceed with text-only brainstorming.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

While you do that — two things I can already tell you about why `aapv-build` builds fail, from the YAML alone:

1. **The stray `/`** in your uncommitted `.buildkite/pipeline.yml:25` (`":shield: Verify Plugin"/`) is invalid YAML. If that's what's committed on the branch Buildkite is building, the pipeline upload itself fails before any step runs.

2. **The `release-draft` step has no Docker image.** Every other step in `pipeline.yml` uses `docker#v5.12.0` with `gradle:9-jdk21`, but `release-draft` runs bare on `queue: default` and calls both `gradle` and `gh`. Unless your agent host has Gradle, a JDK, and the GitHub CLI installed directly, that step fails on `command not found`. It also needs `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which ties back to the secrets question you were answering.

content.text:
I have the full picture now. Before writing anything, here's what I found — the groundwork has some problems worth fixing before adding Qodana.

## State

**All four pipelines already exist** in Buildkite, each pointing at its `.buildkite/pipeline.*.yml`:

| Pipeline | Uploads | Triggers |
|---|---|---|
| `aapv-build` | `pipeline.yml` | branches ✅ PRs ✅ tags ❌ |
| `aapv-qodana` | `pipeline.qodana.yml` | branches ✅ PRs ✅ tags ❌ |
| `aapv-ui-tests` | `pipeline.ui-tests.yml` | branches ✅ PRs ✅ tags ❌ |
| `aapv-release` | `pipeline.release.yml` | branches ✅ PRs ✅ tags ❌ |

None has a branch filter. Compute is a single hosted queue: **`LINUX_AMD64_2X4` — 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, Linux amd64 only.**

Cluster secrets that exist: `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_ACTOR`, `GRADLE_PUBLISH_KEY`, `GRADLE_PUBLISH_SECRET`, `OSSRH_USERNAME`, `OSSRH_PASSWORD`.

## Five problems

1. **Nothing has ever actually run.** All 9 retained builds failed at `pipeline upload` with `no such file or directory` — `.buildkite/` exists only on `migrate-to-buildkite`, and main still has all four GitHub workflows. Whatever green runs you had earlier have aged out of retention, so I can't confirm the build steps ever passed.

2. **Merging as-is fires all four pipelines on every commit** — including `aapv-release`, which publishes to JetBrains Marketplace. That's the one I'd least like to discover by accident.

3. **`aapv-ui-tests` can't run.** Its steps target `os: macos` / `os: windows` / `os: linux` agent tags. Your only queue is hosted Linux with no such tags — the macOS and Windows steps would queue forever.

4. **`aapv-release` can't run.** It keys off `$BUILDKITE_TAG`, but `build_tags` is `false` on that pipeline. It also needs `PUBLISH_TOKEN`, `CERTIFICATE_CHAIN`, `PRIVATE_KEY`, `PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD` — none of which are in the cluster — and calls `gh` inside `gradle:8-jdk21`, which has no `gh` binary.

5. **Secrets aren't wired the way the YAML assumes.** Every pipeline uses `$${QODANA_TOKEN?}` / `$${GITHUB_TOKEN?}`, which expects the var to already be in the job environment. Buildkite cluster secrets aren't auto-injected — they need `buildkite-agent secret get KEY`. So the `release-draft` step in `pipeline.yml` would fail on `GITHUB_TOKEN` even though that secret exists. And `QODANA_TOKEN` isn't in the cluster at all.

Also worth noting: 4 GB RAM is what drove your OOM commits (`buildSearchableOptions`, plugin verifier heap cap). Qodana's JVM analysis on 4 GB is going to be tight — expect to fight that.

And the stray `/` on `pipeline.yml:25` is still uncommitted and would break upload.

## Where I'd go

Qodana is still the right next flow, but I'd sequence one thing ahead of it: **put branch/tag guards on `aapv-release` and `aapv-ui-tests` first**, so merging this branch can't trigger a publish. That's a small change — a `branch_configuration` on each pipeline, plus `build_tags: true` on release — and it de-risks everything after.

content.text:
Two more things surfaced while checking:

- **Linter mismatch.** `qodana.yaml:6` declares `jetbrains/qodana-jvm-community:2025.3`, but `pipeline.qodana.yml` runs `jetbrains/qodana-jvm:2025.3` — the licensed edition, not community. Running the wrong image is a likely first failure.
- `bk secret create --cluster-uuid ... --key ...` exists, so you can add `QODANA_TOKEN` yourself without the value passing through me.

## Design

**Phase 1 — guards, so a merge can't publish**

1. Fix the stray `/` in `.buildkite/pipeline.yml:25`.
2. `aapv-release` → `build_branches: false`, `build_pull_requests: false`, `build_tags: true`. Tag pushes only. It still won't *succeed* (missing secrets, `gh` absent from the Gradle image) — but it can no longer fire on a merge, which is the point. Fixing it properly is a later phase.
3. `aapv-ui-tests` → all three triggers `false`. Manual-only, matching its old `workflow_dispatch`.
4. Rewrite `pipeline.ui-tests.yml` down to the single Linux/Xvfb step; delete the macOS and Windows steps.

*Verification:* re-read both pipelines via the API to confirm settings, then push a commit to this branch and confirm only `aapv-build` and `aapv-qodana` create builds.

**Phase 2 — Qodana to green**

5. You run `bk secret create --cluster-uuid a4da0d9f-be57-4ed3-ac5b-1ccceab79c7b --key QODANA_TOKEN`.
6. Rewrite `pipeline.qodana.yml`: fetch the token via `buildkite-agent secret get` instead of the bare `$${QODANA_TOKEN?}`; switch to the community image to match `qodana.yaml`; replace the fragile `git diff HEAD~1 HEAD` doc-skip with Buildkite's `BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST_BASE_BRANCH`; cap the JVM heap for the 4 GB agent; keep the report in `artifact_paths`.
7. Push and iterate until green. Budget for at least one memory round-trip — 4 GB is tight for Qodana, and it's the same wall you hit with `buildSearchableOptions` and the verifier.

Out of scope for now: fixing release properly, and deleting `.github/workflows/` — both wait until the release flow is migrated.

# Qodana code quality pipeline — replaces .github/workflows/qodana_code_quality.yml
#
# Runs on pull requests and on pushes to main and releases/*, matching the
# triggers the GitHub workflow had. The `if` below does that filtering; the
# aapv-qodana pipeline itself builds all branches and PRs.
#
# Documentation-only changes are skipped, replacing GitHub's paths-ignore.

steps:
  - label: ":qodana: Qodana Scan"
    key: qodana
    if: build.pull_request.id != null || build.branch == "main" || build.branch =~ /^releases\//
    agents:
      queue: default
    timeout_in_minutes: 45
    env:
      QODANA_ENDPOINT: "https://qodana.cloud"
    commands:
      - |
        # Skip documentation-only changes (replaces GitHub's paths-ignore).
        # On a PR, diff against the base branch; on a push, against the parent commit.
        if [ -n "$${BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST_BASE_BRANCH:-}" ]; then
          git fetch -q --no-tags origin "$$BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST_BASE_BRANCH"
          CHANGED="$$(git diff --name-only "origin/$$BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST_BASE_BRANCH...HEAD")"
        else
          CHANGED="$$(git diff --name-only HEAD~1 HEAD 2>/dev/null || true)"
        fi

        # An empty diff means we could not determine the change set — scan rather
        # than silently pass.
        if [ -n "$$CHANGED" ]; then
          NON_DOC="$$(printf '%s\n' "$$CHANGED" \
            | grep -vE '^(CHANGELOG|CONTRIBUTING|CODE_OF_CONDUCT|README)\.md$$' \
            | grep -v '^img/' || true)"
          if [ -z "$$NON_DOC" ]; then
            echo "Only documentation changes detected — skipping Qodana scan."
            exit 0
          fi
        fi
      - |
        # Run Qodana via Docker, mirroring JetBrains/qodana-action.
        #
        # Image must match `linter:` in qodana.yaml — the community edition. The
        # licensed jetbrains/qodana-jvm image will fail the license check.
        #
        # -u keeps report files owned by the agent user so artifact upload and
        # the agent's git clean don't hit root-owned paths.
        #
        # Heap is capped because the hosted queue is LINUX_AMD64_2X4 — 2 vCPU and
        # 4 GB total. Raise only if the agent shape changes.
        QODANA_TOKEN="$$(buildkite-agent secret get QODANA_TOKEN)"

        mkdir -p build/qodana/results build/qodana/report

        docker run --rm \
          -u "$$(id -u):$$(id -g)" \
          -v "$$(pwd):/data/project" \
          -e QODANA_TOKEN="$$QODANA_TOKEN" \
          -e QODANA_ENDPOINT="$$QODANA_ENDPOINT" \
          -e _JAVA_OPTIONS="-Xmx2500m" \
          jetbrains/qodana-jvm-community:2025.3 \
          --save-report \
          --results-dir /data/project/build/qodana/results \
          --report-dir /data/project/build/qodana/report
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/qodana/report/**/*"

Phase 1 and 2 code work is done. Here's where things stand.

**Buildkite changes (applied, verified by reading back):**
- `aapv-release` → `build_branches: false`, `build_pull_requests: false`, `build_tags: true`. Can no longer fire on a merge.
- `aapv-ui-tests` → all three triggers `false`. Manual only.

**File changes:**
- `.buildkite/pipeline.yml` — stray `/` removed (back in sync with HEAD, so it shows no diff).
- `.buildkite/pipeline.ui-tests.yml` — collapsed to one Linux step in a `gradle:9-jdk21` container with Xvfb installed; macOS and Windows legs deleted; the unmet prerequisites documented at the top.
- `.buildkite/pipeline.qodana.yml` — token via `buildkite-agent secret get`, community image to match `qodana.yaml`, `if` condition replacing GitHub's branch triggers, doc-skip rewritten against `BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST_BASE_BRANCH`, heap capped at 2500m, 45-minute timeout.

All four files parse.

**Two things I did not touch**, both in `pipeline.yml`'s `release-draft` step. It has the same secret bug (`$${GITHUB_TOKEN?}` won't resolve from cluster secrets), *and* it runs `gradle` and `gh` bare on a hosted agent with no container — so neither binary is present. Fixing the secret alone won't make it pass, so I left it rather than half-fix it. That's the next piece of work, and it matters: it's the last step of `aapv-build`, so main won't go green without it.

**One thing I need from you** — the Qodana token isn't in the cluster:

```
! bk secret create --cluster-uuid a4da0d9f-be57-4ed3-ac5b-1ccceab79c7b --key QODANA_TOKEN
```

Use the same value as the `QODANA_TOKEN_1066104082` GitHub secret.

I haven't committed anything. Want me to commit these and push, so `aapv-qodana` gets a real run? Note the push will also trigger `aapv-build`, which will still fail at `release-draft` for the reasons above — expected, not a regression.

ci: wire Qodana to cluster secrets, drop unrunnable UI test legs

Qodana:
- Read QODANA_TOKEN via `buildkite-agent secret get` instead of a bare env
  var. Cluster secrets are not auto-injected into the job environment, so
  the previous $${QODANA_TOKEN?} form could never resolve.
- Use jetbrains/qodana-jvm-community:2025.3 to match `linter:` in
  qodana.yaml. The licensed image fails the license check.
- Replace GitHub's branch triggers with a step `if`, and rewrite the
  doc-only skip against BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST_BASE_BRANCH so it works on
  PR builds rather than relying on HEAD~1.
- Cap heap and run as the agent user; the hosted queue is LINUX_AMD64_2X4
  (2 vCPU, 4 GB) and root-owned reports break artifact upload.

UI tests:
- Drop the macOS and Windows legs. The only queue is hosted Linux amd64,
  so those steps would have queued forever waiting for agents.
- Run the Linux leg in a container with Xvfb, matching the other pipelines.
- Document that this cannot pass yet: `runIdeForUiTests` does not exist
  (renamed to testIdeUi in IJPGP 2.x) and the build declares
  TestFrameworkType.Platform rather than Starter.

Pipeline triggers were also guarded in Buildkite so a merge cannot fire a
publish: aapv-release is now tags-only, aapv-ui-tests is manual-only.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

Real data now. Build 56 final:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| pipeline upload | **passed** — first successful upload ever |
| Test (`gradle check`) | **passed** |
| Build (`buildPlugin`) | **passed** |
| Verify Plugin | **failed** — OOM |

So the migration substantially works. Two steps are genuinely green for the first time.

**Why Verify OOMs.** The 4 GB agent can't fit what's being asked of it:

- `gradle.properties:15` — `org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx2048m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m` → up to 2.5 GB
- `gradle.properties:14` — `kotlin.daemon.jvmargs=-Xmx2048m` → another 2 GB
- plus the IntelliJ Plugin Verifier, which forks its *own* JVM on top

That's already over 4 GB before the verifier allocates anything. Note commit `0f11d0b` capped the verifier at 1 GB via `freeArgs`, and `4f257bd` removed `freeArgs` because it corrupted the verifier's CLI args — so **the heap cap is currently gone**. That regression is precisely what you're hitting.

The clean fix isn't `freeArgs`: in IntelliJ Platform Gradle Plugin 2.x, `verifyPlugin` is a `JavaExec` task, so `maxHeapSize` can be set directly on it without touching CLI args. Combined with lowering the Gradle/Kotlin heaps for CI only, that should fit.

**Also worth knowing:**

- **Qodana still hasn't run.** I installed its webhook (hook `662861870`), but webhooks only fire on new events, and there's been no push since. It also still needs the secret — `QODANA_TOKEN` is not in the cluster yet, so the step would fail at `buildkite-agent secret get`. Add it and I'll push a trivial commit to trigger a run.
- **`aapv-release` and `aapv-ui-tests` correctly produced no builds** — the guards work.
- **Build 55 ran on branch `entire/checkpoints/v1`** and failed. The `entire` tool pushes that branch, and `aapv-build` builds all branches, so you're burning agent minutes on checkpoint pushes. A `branch_configuration` excluding it would stop that.

---
name: buildkite-ci-topology
description: Buildkite org/cluster/queue IDs and pipeline wiring for the A2PT plugin CI, plus which settings the REST API cannot change
metadata:
  type: project
---

CI for this repo runs in Buildkite org `z8dn` (migration from GitHub Actions began on branch `migrate-to-buildkite`, PR #48).

- Cluster `a4da0d9f-be57-4ed3-ac5b-1ccceab79c7b` ("Default cluster"), single queue `default` = `6069f2e4-0dae-42b5-ada6-36a76366d092`, Buildkite **hosted** agents.
- Four pipelines, each uploading its own file: `aapv-build` → `.buildkite/pipeline.yml`, `aapv-qodana` → `pipeline.qodana.yml`, `aapv-release` → `pipeline.release.yml`, `aapv-ui-tests` → `pipeline.ui-tests.yml`.

Three things that are easy to get wrong here:

1. **Every pipeline needs its own GitHub webhook.** Buildkite issues a distinct webhook URL per pipeline. For a long time only `aapv-build`'s hook was installed on the repo, so the other three pipelines received zero events and never built. Check `gh api repos/z8dn/advanced-android-project-view/hooks` against each pipeline's `provider.webhook_url` before concluding a pipeline is misconfigured.
2. **Cluster secrets are not auto-injected into the job environment.** They must be read with `buildkite-agent secret get KEY`. Pipeline YAML written as `$${SOME_TOKEN?}` will never resolve, even when the secret exists in the cluster. List them with `bk secret list --cluster-uuid <uuid>`.
3. **Hosted agent instance shape cannot be changed via the REST API.** `PATCH .../queues/<uuid>` silently ignores a `hosted_agents` body and returns the old shape; `bk queue update` only exposes `--description` and `--retry-agent-affinity`. Change it in the web UI under the cluster's queue settings.

The `bk` CLI stores its token in the macOS keychain, so `bk` calls need `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` — under the sandbox every REST call returns 401 even though `~/.config/bk.yaml` looks configured.

See [[a2pt-ci-memory-constraints]] for why agent RAM is the recurring failure mode.

---
name: a2pt-ci-memory-constraints
description: Why A2PT's CI keeps hitting OOM — the Gradle/Kotlin/verifier heap budget versus the hosted agent size
metadata:
  type: project
---

Nearly every CI failure on this plugin traces back to agent RAM, not to the code. The default hosted queue was `LINUX_AMD64_2X4` (2 vCPU / 4 GB) as of 2026-08-08, while a single `verifyPlugin` run wants more than that on its own:

- `gradle.properties` sets `org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx2048m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m` (up to 2.5 GB)
- `gradle.properties` also sets `kotlin.daemon.jvmargs=-Xmx2048m` (another 2 GB)
- the IntelliJ Plugin Verifier then forks a *third* JVM on top

The symptom is `Gradle build daemon disappeared unexpectedly` — the OOM killer, not a Gradle bug. Same root cause as the earlier decision to skip `buildSearchableOptions` in CI.

Commit `0f11d0b` capped the verifier heap at 1 GB using `freeArgs`, but `4f257bd` removed `freeArgs` because it corrupted the verifier's CLI arguments — so **the cap is currently gone**. The clean way to re-apply it is `maxHeapSize` on the `verifyPlugin` task directly (it is a `JavaExec` under IntelliJ Platform Gradle Plugin 2.x), *not* `freeArgs`.

**Why:** the repo's own Gradle config is tuned for a developer laptop, and nothing in it signals that CI has a quarter of that memory.

**How to apply:** when a CI step dies with no useful stack trace, check the agent shape first (see [[buildkite-ci-topology]]) before debugging the Gradle build itself.

content.text:
Confirmed on the real source — `VerifyPluginTask.kt:51`:

```kotlin
abstract class VerifyPluginTask : JavaExec(), RuntimeAware, PluginVerifierAware, ProblemsAware
```

It's a `JavaExec`, so `maxHeapSize` is directly settable, and it **forks its own JVM**. That also explains the `freeArgs` regression precisely: line 331 appends `freeArgs` to the verifier's *CLI* args, not the JVM's — so `-Xmx1g` went to the verifier binary as a command-line flag and corrupted it. Commit `4f257bd` was right to remove it; the mechanism was just wrong.

Nothing sets a default heap, so the forked verifier gets the JVM default of ¼ physical RAM.

## The actual budget

That's what's blowing up. On a 4 GB agent, `verifyPlugin` transitively runs `buildPlugin`, so three JVMs are live:

| JVM | Heap | ~RSS |
|---|---|---|
| Gradle daemon | `-Xmx2048m` + 512m metaspace | ~2.8 GB |
| Kotlin daemon | `-Xmx2048m` | ~2.3 GB |
| Forked verifier | default ¼ RAM = 1 GB | ~1.2 GB |

Peak ≈ 6.3 GB against 4 GB. The OOM killer takes the Gradle daemon, which surfaces as `daemon disappeared unexpectedly`.

## What fits without upgrading

Three changes, all free:

1. **`tasks.verifyPlugin { maxHeapSize = "1536m" }`** in `build.gradle.kts` — the correct replacement for the reverted `freeArgs` cap. Note this sets it *higher* than the 1 GB default, not lower: the verifier is the one process that genuinely needs headroom to load Android Studio.
2. **`-Dkotlin.compiler.execution.strategy=in-process`** on the CI step — removes the separate 2.3 GB Kotlin daemon entirely, folding compilation into the Gradle daemon. This is the single biggest win.
3. **`-Dorg.gradle.jvmargs="-Xmx1024m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=384m"`** on the CI step only, leaving `gradle.properties` alone so your local builds keep their current settings.

New peak ≈ 3.4 GB. It fits, but not comfortably — and in-process Kotlin compilation pushes pressure into that smaller Gradle heap, so there's some chance it just moves the failure. I'd call it likely-to-work, not certain.

Worth being straight about the trade: the upgrade costs money and definitively solves it; this costs nothing and probably solves it. They're also not exclusive — capping heaps is good hygiene either way, and it's the only one of the two that fixes the `freeArgs` regression still sitting in your build file.

it works, but what is the buildkite-agent pipeline upload .buildkite/pipeline.yml step

That's the bootstrap step — it's what makes your pipeline definition live in the repo instead of in Buildkite's UI.

**How it works.** A Buildkite pipeline stores its steps in Buildkite itself. Yours stores exactly one:

```
buildkite-agent pipeline upload .buildkite/pipeline.yml
```

When a build starts, Buildkite has only that step. An agent picks it up, checks out the repo at the commit being built, and runs it. `pipeline upload` reads the YAML **out of that checkout** and POSTs the steps back to the Buildkite API, which appends them to the build that's already running. The build grows itself at runtime.

That's the `:pipeline:` job you saw in build 56's job list, and why it always appears first and takes under a second.

**Why it's done this way.** Your steps get versioned, diffed, and code-reviewed like anything else. A PR that changes `.buildkite/pipeline.yml` is tested with its own changes applied, because the upload reads the PR's checkout. If steps lived in the UI, you'd be editing CI config in a web form with no history.

It's also why your four pipelines can share one repo — each one's stored step uploads a *different* file:

| Pipeline | Stored step |
|---|---|
| `aapv-build` | `pipeline upload .buildkite/pipeline.yml` |
| `aapv-qodana` | `pipeline upload .buildkite/pipeline.qodana.yml` |
| `aapv-release` | `pipeline upload .buildkite/pipeline.release.yml` |
| `aapv-ui-tests` | `pipeline upload .buildkite/pipeline.ui-tests.yml` |

**This is exactly what was failing before.** Build 54 ran on `main`, where `.buildkite/` doesn't exist yet:

```
buildkite-agent: fatal: failed to read file: open .buildkite/pipeline.yml: no such file or directory
```

The upload step was the *only* step, so when it failed the build had nothing else to run and died in 0.6 seconds. Nothing was broken about your Gradle setup — Buildkite just never got a step list.

**Two things worth knowing:**

- The path is the default. Bare `buildkite-agent pipeline upload` looks for `.buildkite/pipeline.yml` on its own. Being explicit is fine and clearer given you have four files.
- You can call it more than once, and from a script. Since it just reads stdin or a file, you can generate steps programmatically — `./generate-steps.sh | buildkite-agent pipeline upload` — which is how people fan out per-package or per-test-shard builds. You don't need that here, but it's the reason the mechanism exists in this shape.

One caveat that will bite eventually: step filters like the `if:` I added to the Qodana step and `branches: "main"` on release-draft are evaluated **at upload time**, against the build's branch and PR metadata. A step that's filtered out is uploaded and then marked `broken` — that's the state you saw on Create Release Draft, and it means "skipped by a filter", not "failed".

i see. Is this the idiomatic way to do buildkite in github ?

Mostly yes on the mechanics, no on the topology.

## What you have is idiomatic

- **The `pipeline upload` bootstrap.** Universal Buildkite practice. Every repo does this.
- **YAML in `.buildkite/`.** Standard path, standard layout.
- **The `docker#v5.12.0` plugin for toolchain.** This is the normal way to get a JDK onto an agent that doesn't have one. Baking tools into a custom agent image is the alternative, but the plugin is the common starting point.
- **`buildkite-agent secret get`.** Current idiom for hosted agents. The `$${VAR?}` form your files had is the older self-hosted pattern where an agent `environment` hook exports vars.

## What isn't

**Four pipelines for one repo is the unusual part.** Buildkite's normal unit is one pipeline per repo. You'd express variation *inside* `pipeline.yml` with `if:` conditions, or with `trigger` steps that fire a genuinely separate pipeline.

The costs you've already paid for this are exactly the predictable ones: four webhooks to install (you were missing three), four independent sets of trigger settings to keep in sync, and four places to look when something doesn't fire. That's not a hypothetical — it's the bug we spent this session finding.

The idiomatic shape for chaining is a `trigger` step, not a second webhook:

```yaml
- trigger: aapv-release
  label: ":rocket: Release"
  branches: "main"
  build:
    commit: "$BUILDKITE_COMMIT"
```

That gives the release its own pipeline and build page — which is genuinely nice for a publish flow — without a second webhook or a second copy of the trigger config.

**Your steps rebuild instead of sharing artifacts.** This is the more consequential one. Right now Test, Build, and Verify run concurrently and each compiles the plugin from scratch — three full Kotlin compiles per commit. Idiomatic Buildkite is build-once-then-fan-out:

```yaml
- label: ":hammer: Build"
  key: build
  artifact_paths: "build/distributions/*.zip"

- label: ":shield: Verify"
  depends_on: build
  commands:
    - buildkite-agent artifact download "build/distributions/*.zip" .
    - ...
```

`depends_on` is the modern form; the bare `wait` you have is the older style and creates a hard barrier across *all* steps rather than expressing real dependencies.

Note this connects straight back to the OOM. Verify only blew past 4 GB because it ran `buildPlugin` itself and spun up a Kotlin daemon. If it downloaded the artifact instead, that JVM wouldn't exist and the memory problem would largely evaporate — the heap flags I just added are compensating for work the step shouldn't be doing.

**One thing you're missing that's very idiomatic:** `buildkite-agent annotate`. It renders markdown on the build page, and it's how people surface verifier findings or test failures without making you dig through logs. For a plugin verifier that emits a structured report, it's a natural fit.

## The honest summary

Your migration is a faithful *translation* of the GitHub Actions layout — four workflows became four pipelines, and each job kept doing its own full build because that's what GitHub jobs must do (they're separate VMs with no shared state). Buildkite doesn't have that constraint, so the translation carries over costs that don't need to exist.

That's a reasonable place to be mid-migration. Getting it green first was the right call. But if you want it to read as Buildkite rather than as transliterated Actions, the consolidation is the next step.

Want me to sketch what a single-pipeline version looks like? It'd be one `pipeline.yml` with artifact passing and `depends_on`, Qodana as a conditional step, and a `trigger` step for release — collapsing four webhooks to one.

  # Requires PUBLISH_TOKEN, CERTIFICATE_CHAIN, PRIVATE_KEY and
  # PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD as cluster secrets. They do not exist yet, so this step
  # will fail until they are added:
  #   bk secret create --cluster-uuid <uuid> --key PUBLISH_TOKEN
  - label: ":rocket: Publish Plugin"
    key: publish
    if: build.tag != null
    plugins: &gradle_docker
      - docker#v5.12.0:
          image: "gradle:9-jdk21"
          mount-buildkite-agent: true
    commands:
      - apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq gh
      - |
        export GITHUB_TOKEN="$$(buildkite-agent secret get GITHUB_TOKEN)"
        export PUBLISH_TOKEN="$$(buildkite-agent secret get PUBLISH_TOKEN)"
        export CERTIFICATE_CHAIN="$$(buildkite-agent secret get CERTIFICATE_CHAIN)"
        export PRIVATE_KEY="$$(buildkite-agent secret get PRIVATE_KEY)"
        export PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD="$$(buildkite-agent secret get PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD)"

        TAG="$$BUILDKITE_TAG"

        # Strip leading blank lines from the release notes, matching the sed in
        # the old workflow.
        CHANGELOG="$$(gh release view "$$TAG" --json body -q '.body' \
          | sed -e 's/^[[:space:]]*$$//g' -e '/./,$$!d')"

        if [ -n "$$CHANGELOG" ]; then
          gradle patchChangelog --release-note="$$CHANGELOG"
        fi

        gradle publishPlugin
        gh release upload "$$TAG" ./build/distributions/*

        if [ -n "$$CHANGELOG" ]; then
          BRANCH="changelog-update-$$TAG"

          git config user.email "buildkite@ci"
          git config user.name "Buildkite"
          git checkout -b "$$BRANCH"
          git commit -am "Changelog update - $$TAG"
          git push --set-upstream origin "$$BRANCH"

          gh label create "release changelog" \
            --description "Pull requests with release changelog update" \
            --force || true

          gh pr create \
            --title "Changelog update - \`$$TAG\`" \
            --body "Current pull request contains patched \`CHANGELOG.md\` file for the \`$$TAG\` version." \
            --label "release changelog" \
            --head "$$BRANCH"
        fi
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/distributions/*.zip"

  # ─── Everything below is for non-tag builds ────────────────────────────────

  - label: ":hammer: Build"
    key: build
    if: build.tag == null
    # buildSearchableOptions launches a full IntelliJ IDE and needs ~4GB. It only
    # generates marketplace search indexes, so it is skipped on CI.
    command: "gradle buildPlugin -x buildSearchableOptions"
    plugins: *gradle_docker
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/distributions/*.zip"

  - label: ":test_tube: Test"
    key: test
    if: build.tag == null
    command: "gradle check"
    plugins: *gradle_docker
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/reports/tests/**/*"
      - "build/reports/kover/report.xml"

  - label: ":shield: Verify Plugin"
    key: verify
    if: build.tag == null
    depends_on: build
    plugins: *gradle_docker
    commands:
      - buildkite-agent artifact download "build/distributions/*.zip" .
      - |
        # Point the verifier at the artifact the Build step produced and exclude
        # buildPlugin, so this step neither recompiles nor starts a Kotlin
        # daemon. Three JVMs at once is what previously exhausted the agent and
        # showed up as "Gradle build daemon disappeared unexpectedly".
        ARCHIVE="$$(ls build/distributions/*.zip | head -1)"
        echo "Verifying $$ARCHIVE"

        gradle verifyPlugin \
          -PverifyArchive="$$ARCHIVE" \
          -x buildPlugin \
          -x buildSearchableOptions \
          --no-daemon --max-workers 1 \
          -Dorg.gradle.jvmargs="-Xmx1024m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=384m"
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/reports/pluginVerifier/**/*"

  # Replaces .github/workflows/qodana_code_quality.yml. Runs on pull requests and
  # on pushes to main and releases/*, and skips documentation-only changes in
  # place of GitHub's paths-ignore.
  - label: ":qodana: Qodana Scan"
    key: qodana
    if: build.tag == null && (build.pull_request.id != null || build.branch == "main" || build.branch =~ /^releases\//)
    timeout_in_minutes: 45
    env:
      QODANA_ENDPOINT: "https://qodana.cloud"
    commands:
      - |
        # On a PR, diff against the base branch; on a push, against the parent.
        if [ -n "$${BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST_BASE_BRANCH:-}" ]; then
          git fetch -q --no-tags origin "$$BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST_BASE_BRANCH"
          CHANGED="$$(git diff --name-only "origin/$$BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST_BASE_BRANCH...HEAD")"
        else
          CHANGED="$$(git diff --name-only HEAD~1 HEAD 2>/dev/null || true)"
        fi

        # An empty diff means the change set could not be determined — scan
        # rather than silently pass.
        if [ -n "$$CHANGED" ]; then
          NON_DOC="$$(printf '%s\n' "$$CHANGED" \
            | grep -vE '^(CHANGELOG|CONTRIBUTING|CODE_OF_CONDUCT|README)\.md$$' \
            | grep -v '^img/' || true)"
          if [ -z "$$NON_DOC" ]; then
            echo "Only documentation changes detected — skipping Qodana scan."
            exit 0
          fi
        fi
      - |
        # Image must match `linter:` in qodana.yaml — the community edition. The
        # licensed jetbrains/qodana-jvm image fails the license check.
        #
        # -u keeps report files owned by the agent user, so artifact upload and
        # the agent's git clean do not trip over root-owned paths.
        QODANA_TOKEN="$$(buildkite-agent secret get QODANA_TOKEN)"

        mkdir -p build/qodana/results build/qodana/report

        docker run --rm \
          -u "$$(id -u):$$(id -g)" \
          -v "$$(pwd):/data/project" \
          -e QODANA_TOKEN="$$QODANA_TOKEN" \
          -e QODANA_ENDPOINT="$$QODANA_ENDPOINT" \
          -e _JAVA_OPTIONS="-Xmx2500m" \
          jetbrains/qodana-jvm-community:2025.3 \
          --save-report \
          --results-dir /data/project/build/qodana/results \
          --report-dir /data/project/build/qodana/report
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/qodana/report/**/*"

  # Replaces .github/workflows/run-ui-tests.yml, which was workflow_dispatch only.
  # Start with: bk build create -e RUN_UI_TESTS=true
  #
  # WARNING: this cannot pass yet. There is no `runIdeForUiTests` task — IntelliJ
  # Platform Gradle Plugin 2.x renamed it to `testIdeUi`, which additionally
  # requires testFramework(TestFrameworkType.Starter) and intellij-ui-test-robot.
  # build.gradle.kts currently declares TestFrameworkType.Platform only.
  #
  # Linux only: the sole hosted queue is linux/amd64, so the macOS and Windows
  # legs of the original matrix had no agents to run on.
  - label: ":linux: UI Tests"
    key: ui-tests
    if: build.env("RUN_UI_TESTS") == "true"
    env:
      DISPLAY: ":99.0"
    plugins:
      - docker#v5.12.0:
          image: "gradle:9-jdk21"
          mount-buildkite-agent: true
          environment:
            - DISPLAY
    commands:
      # The gradle image is Debian-based and runs as root; Xvfb is not included.
      - apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq xvfb curl
      - Xvfb -ac :99 -screen 0 1920x1080x16 &
      - gradle runIdeForUiTests --no-daemon --max-workers 1 &
      - |
        # Wait for the IDE's robot-server (replaces url-health-check-action)
        for i in $$(seq 1 15); do
          if curl -sf http://127.0.0.1:8082 > /dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "IDE is ready"
            break
          fi
          echo "Attempt $$i/15 — waiting 30s..."
          sleep 30
        done
      - gradle test --no-daemon --max-workers 1
    artifact_paths:
      - "build/reports/tests/**/*"

  # ─── Release draft, once CI is green on main ───────────────────────────────
  - label: ":github: Create Release Draft"
    key: release-draft
    branches: "main"
    depends_on:
      - test
      - verify
    plugins: *gradle_docker
    commands:
      - apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq gh
      - |
        export GITHUB_TOKEN="$$(buildkite-agent secret get GITHUB_TOKEN)"

        PROPERTIES="$$(gradle properties --console=plain -q)"
        VERSION="$$(echo "$$PROPERTIES" | grep "^version:" | cut -f2- -d ' ')"
        CHANGELOG="$$(gradle getChangelog --unreleased --no-header --console=plain -q)"

        gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases \
          --jq '.[] | select(.draft == true) | .id' \
          | xargs -I '{}' gh api -X DELETE repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases/{}

        gh release create "v$$VERSION" \
          --draft \
          --title "v$$VERSION" \
          --notes "$$CHANGELOG"

ci: consolidate four Buildkite pipelines into one

The migration translated four GitHub Actions workflows into four Buildkite
pipelines, which carried over constraints that only exist on Actions. Each
pipeline needed its own GitHub webhook — three were never installed, so
aapv-qodana, aapv-release and aapv-ui-tests had never received an event or
run a single build. Trigger settings also had to be kept in sync across four
places.

Everything now lives in .buildkite/pipeline.yml, selected with `if:`:

  branch / PR   build, test, verify, qodana
  main          ...plus the release draft
  tag           publish to JetBrains Marketplace, nothing else
  manual        UI tests, via RUN_UI_TESTS=true

Verify no longer rebuilds. It downloads the Build step's artifact and points
the verifier at it with -PverifyArchive, excluding buildPlugin. archiveFile's
convention is buildPlugin's output provider, so overriding it with a plain
path drops the implicit task dependency — which means no second compile and
no Kotlin daemon, removing the memory pressure at its source rather than
tuning heaps around it.

release-draft now depends_on test and verify instead of relying on a global
`wait`, and both it and publish run in the Gradle image with gh installed;
previously release-draft called gradle and gh on a bare agent where neither
binary exists, and read GITHUB_TOKEN as a plain env var, which never resolves
for cluster secrets.

Buildkite side: aapv-build now builds tags, and the redundant aapv-qodana
webhook has been removed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF

content.text:
Confirmed by the log:

```
Successfully downloaded "Advanced Android Project Tree-0.0.8.zip" 79 KiB
Verifying build/distributions/Advanced Android Project Tree-0.0.8.zip
INFO verification - Reading plugin to check from /workdir/build/distributions/...zip
BUILD SUCCESSFUL in 1m 43s
2 actionable tasks: 2 executed
```

**2 actionable tasks** — no compile, no Kotlin daemon. The verifier read the artifact the Build step produced. Verify went from OOM-death to passing in 1m43s, and `mount-buildkite-agent` correctly bind-mounted the agent binary into the container.

**You don't need the agent upgrade.** I never managed to apply it, and it turns out it was treating a symptom — the memory pressure came from Verify redundantly recompiling, not from the workload being genuinely too big for 4 GB. Leave the queue on `LINUX_AMD64_2X4`.

Build 58, one pipeline, one webhook:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| Publish Plugin | `broken` — skipped, not a tag |
| Build | **passed** |
| Test | **passed** |
| Verify Plugin | **passed** |
| Qodana Scan | failed — `404 Secret not found` |
| UI Tests | `broken` — skipped, `RUN_UI_TESTS` unset |
| Create Release Draft | `broken` — skipped, not main |

Every condition resolved as designed. The one genuine failure is the missing secret:

```
! bk secret create --cluster-uuid a4da0d9f-be57-4ed3-ac5b-1ccceab79c7b --key QODANA_TOKEN
```

Also worth noting the heap flags I added in the previous commit are now largely vestigial — `-x buildPlugin` removed the JVM that was causing the problem. I left them as cheap insurance, but `maxHeapSize` on `verifyPlugin` is the one that still earns its place, since it fixes the reverted `freeArgs` regression.

One cleanup decision left:

questions.question: What should happen to the three now-redundant Buildkite pipelines?

options.label: Archive them (Recommended)
options.description: Archive aapv-qodana, aapv-ui-tests and aapv-release. They stop appearing in the pipeline list but their settings and history are recoverable if you ever want to split something back out. None has a webhook now, so all three are already inert.

options.label: Delete them
options.description: Remove the three pipelines outright. Cleanest list, but irreversible — settings and build history go with them. They have no successful builds between them, so there is little history to lose.

options.label: Leave them for now
options.description: Keep them as-is. They have no webhooks so they cannot trigger, but they will clutter the pipeline list and may confuse someone later.

input.content:
---
name: buildkite-ci-topology
description: Buildkite org/cluster/queue IDs for the A2PT plugin CI, the single-pipeline design, and which settings the REST API cannot change
metadata:
  type: project
---

CI runs in Buildkite org `z8dn`. Migrated off GitHub Actions on branch `migrate-to-buildkite` (PR #48).

- **One pipeline: `aapv`** (renamed from `aapv-build` on 2026-08-08), uploading `.buildkite/pipeline.yml`. Builds branches, PRs and tags; `branch_configuration` is `!entire/checkpoints/*` to ignore the `entire` tool's checkpoint pushes.
- Cluster `a4da0d9f-be57-4ed3-ac5b-1ccceab79c7b`, single queue `default` = `6069f2e4-0dae-42b5-ada6-36a76366d092`, Buildkite **hosted** agents on `LINUX_AMD64_2X4` (2 vCPU / 4 GB, linux/amd64 only — no macOS or Windows).

The migration first created four pipelines mirroring the four GitHub workflows; they were consolidated into one because **each Buildkite pipeline needs its own GitHub webhook**, three were never installed, and those pipelines had therefore never run. Variation now lives in `if:` conditions on steps (tag → publish, main → release draft, PR/main → qodana, `RUN_UI_TESTS=true` → UI tests). If a pipeline seems not to fire, check `gh api repos/z8dn/advanced-android-project-view/hooks` against its `provider.webhook_url` before anything else.

Gotchas worth remembering:

- **Cluster secrets are not auto-injected into the job environment.** Read them with `buildkite-agent secret get KEY`. YAML written as `$${SOME_TOKEN?}` never resolves. List with `bk secret list --cluster-uuid <uuid>`. A missing secret surfaces as a `404 Secret not found`, not a syntax error.
- **`if:` and `branches:` are mutually exclusive on a step.** Put the branch restriction inside the condition.
- A step skipped by `if:` shows as **`broken`**, which means "filtered out", not "failed".
- Using `buildkite-agent` inside a step that uses the docker plugin requires `mount-buildkite-agent: true`.
- **Hosted agent instance shape cannot be changed via the REST API.** `PATCH .../queues/<uuid>` silently ignores a `hosted_agents` body and returns the old shape; `bk queue update` only exposes `--description` and `--retry-agent-affinity`. Use the web UI. Renaming a pipeline, by contrast, works via PATCH and preserves the webhook URL.
- The `bk` CLI keeps its token in the macOS keychain, so `bk` calls need `dangerouslyDisableSandbox` — under the sandbox every REST call returns 401 even though `~/.config/bk.yaml` looks fine.

See [[a2pt-ci-memory-constraints]] for the memory design that lets this fit on a 4 GB agent.

---
name: a2pt-ci-memory-constraints
description: Why A2PT's CI hit OOM and how the artifact-reuse design fixed it without a bigger agent
metadata:
  type: project
---

CI failures on this plugin used to trace back to agent RAM rather than to the code. The symptom is `Gradle build daemon disappeared unexpectedly` — that is the OOM killer, not a Gradle bug.

The cause was three JVMs alive at once in the verify step, against a 4 GB agent:

- Gradle daemon — `org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx2048m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=512m` (~2.8 GB)
- Kotlin daemon — `kotlin.daemon.jvmargs=-Xmx2048m` (~2.3 GB)
- the forked plugin verifier (~1.2 GB)

**Resolved 2026-08-08 by not rebuilding.** `VerifyPluginTask.archiveFile` is an `@InputFile` whose *convention* is `buildPlugin`'s output provider — that provider is what creates the implicit task dependency. `build.gradle.kts` now overrides it with a plain path when `-PverifyArchive` is set, so CI downloads the Build step's artifact and runs `gradle verifyPlugin -PverifyArchive=... -x buildPlugin`. No compile, no Kotlin daemon: the step dropped to **2 actionable tasks, 1m43s**, and passes on the unchanged 4 GB agent. Upgrading the agent was considered and proved unnecessary.

`verifyPlugin` also sets `maxHeapSize = "1536m"`, because a `JavaExec` with no explicit heap inherits a quarter of physical RAM — too little to load Android Studio. **Never set this via `intellijPlatform.pluginVerification.freeArgs`**: those are appended to the verifier's own CLI arguments rather than the JVM's, which is why `0f11d0b` had to be reverted in `4f257bd`.

`buildSearchableOptions` remains excluded on CI — it launches a full IDE and wants ~4 GB on its own.

**Why:** `gradle.properties` is tuned for a developer laptop and gives no hint that CI has a quarter of that memory.

**How to apply:** when a CI step dies with no useful stack trace, suspect memory, and prefer removing duplicated work over raising heaps or agent size. See [[buildkite-ci-topology]] for the agent shape.

Done. You're on one pipeline.

**Buildkite now:**
- `aapv` (renamed from `aapv-build`) — builds branches, PRs, and tags; ignores `entire/checkpoints/*`
- `aapv-qodana`, `aapv-ui-tests`, `aapv-release` — deleted
- One GitHub webhook, and I verified the URL is byte-identical after the rename, so it keeps working. `branch_configuration`, trigger settings, and the upload step all survived.

**The consolidation works** (build 58): Build, Test, and Verify all passed on the original 4 GB agent. Publish, UI Tests, and Release Draft each showed `broken`, which is Buildkite's state for "filtered out by `if:`" — exactly right for a non-tag, non-main branch build.

The Verify fix is the substantive one. It downloads the Build step's artifact and points the verifier at it, so the step ran **2 actionable tasks in 1m43s** instead of recompiling the plugin. That removed the third JVM, which was the actual cause of the OOM — so **skip the agent upgrade**, it was treating a symptom.

**Two things still open:**

1. **Qodana needs its secret.** It's the only genuinely failing step, with a clean `404 Secret not found`:
   ```
   ! bk secret create --cluster-uuid a4da0d9f-be57-4ed3-ac5b-1ccceab79c7b --key QODANA_TOKEN
   ```

2. **The release path is written but unproven.** `publish` is gated on tags and needs `PUBLISH_TOKEN`, `CERTIFICATE_CHAIN`, `PRIVATE_KEY`, and `PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD`, none of which exist in the cluster. `release-draft` is gated on main and no build has reached it yet. Both now run in the Gradle image with `gh` installed and read `GITHUB_TOKEN` via `buildkite-agent secret get`, which fixes the bugs I flagged earlier — but neither has actually executed, so treat them as untested.

Also still true: `.github/workflows/` is untouched on `main`, so both CI systems will run once PR #48 merges. Deleting those four files is the last step of the migration, and worth doing in the same merge to avoid double-billing.

content.text:
Qodana says it outright:

```
✗ Qodana was terminated after running out of memory.
```

But look at what it's doing right before dying:

```
[IDE]: Task 'Analyzing project to enable smart features' ended
[Gradle]: Download .../android-studio-quail1-canary1-linux.tar.gz, took 35s
Keep running Project opening ... so far 1m 30s
```

Qodana performs a **full Gradle project import**, which makes IJPGP resolve and download the entire Android Studio distribution inside the Qodana container. So that container is holding Qodana's own analyzer JVM, a Gradle daemon, and an unpacked Android Studio — in 4 GB.

**And I made it worse.** I set `_JAVA_OPTIONS=-Xmx2500m`, which is inherited by *every* JVM spawned in the container, not just Qodana's. The Gradle daemon doing that import also claimed a 2500m heap. That was the wrong knob; a targeted setting was needed.

This one is not like `verifyPlugin`. There's no duplicated work to remove — Qodana needs the project model, and the project model needs the Android Studio SDK. JetBrains recommends 8 GB for the JVM linters. Let me check whether a second, larger queue is possible so only Qodana pays for it.

content.text:
Neither `bk queue create` nor `bk queue update` can set an instance shape — same REST gap as before, so any larger queue has to be made in the web UI.

Removing `_JAVA_OPTIONS` is right regardless. The rest depends on how you want to pay for Qodana's memory.

questions.question: How should Qodana get the memory it needs?

options.label: Second, larger queue (Recommended)
options.description: Create a `large` queue at LINUX_AMD64_8X16 in the UI; target only the Qodana step with `agents: queue: large`. Build/Test/Verify stay on the cheap 2x4, so you pay the higher rate for one step a few times a day rather than for every step. I'd write the YAML; you'd create the queue.

options.label: Upgrade the single queue
options.description: Move the existing `default` queue to 8x16. Simplest config, one queue to reason about, and it would let you re-enable buildSearchableOptions. But every step then bills at the higher rate, including short ones.

options.label: Run Qodana outside CI
options.description: Drop the step and use Qodana Cloud's own scanning or run it locally before releases. Costs nothing in Buildkite and sidesteps the memory problem, but you lose per-PR code-quality feedback.

options.label: Qodana on main only
options.description: Keep it in the pipeline but restrict it to pushes to main rather than every PR, cutting how often the memory is needed. Still needs a bigger agent when it does run, so this pairs with one of the first two.

content.text:
Diagnosed and committed, not yet pushed.

**What killed it:** not the token — that part worked. Qodana runs a full Gradle project import, which makes IJPGP resolve and unpack the entire Android Studio distribution *inside* the Qodana container, on top of Qodana's own analyzer JVM. In 4 GB that's hopeless.

This is genuinely unlike the `verifyPlugin` fix. There I removed duplicated work — Verify was recompiling something another step had already built. Here there's nothing redundant to strip: the analysis needs the project model, and the project model needs the SDK. It just wants more memory.

**I also had a bug in it.** `_JAVA_OPTIONS=-Xmx2500m` is inherited by *every* JVM the container spawns, so it was capping the Gradle daemon doing the import too — pushing it toward failure rather than away. Removed; JVM ergonomics reads the cgroup limit and sizes better than a fixed number.

**Your turn — create the queue** (the API can't set instance shape):

1. https://buildkite.com/organizations/z8dn/clusters/a4da0d9f-be57-4ed3-ac5b-1ccceab79c7b

**Resolved 2026-08-08 by not rebuilding.** `VerifyPluginTask.archiveFile` is an `@InputFile` whose *convention* is `buildPlugin`'s output provider — that provider is what creates the implicit task dependency. `build.gradle.kts` now overrides it with a plain path when `-PverifyArchive` is set, so CI downloads the Build step's artifact and runs `gradle verifyPlugin -PverifyArchive=... -x buildPlugin`. No compile, no Kotlin daemon: the step dropped to **2 actionable tasks, 1m43s**, and passes on the unchanged 4 GB agent. Upgrading the agent was considered and proved unnecessary.

`verifyPlugin` also sets `maxHeapSize = "1536m"`, because a `JavaExec` with no explicit heap inherits a quarter of physical RAM — too little to load Android Studio. **Never set this via `intellijPlatform.pluginVerification.freeArgs`**: those are appended to the verifier's own CLI arguments rather than the JVM's, which is why `0f11d0b` had to be reverted in `4f257bd`.
input.new_string:
**Resolved 2026-08-08 by not rebuilding.** CI downloads the Build step's artifact and runs `gradle verifyPlugin -x buildPlugin`. No compile, no Kotlin daemon: the step dropped to **2 actionable tasks, 1m43s**, and passes on the unchanged 4 GB agent. Upgrading the agent was considered and proved unnecessary.

Excluding `buildPlugin` is safe with no build-script support, because `verifyPlugin.archiveFile` is an `@InputFile` whose convention is `buildPlugin.archiveFile` — which resolves to `build/distributions/<name>-<version>.zip`, exactly where `buildkite-agent artifact download` lands it. Gradle only needs the input present at execution time. (An explicit `-PverifyArchive` override was tried and then reverted as unnecessary; `build.gradle.kts` has no `verifyPlugin` block.)

If the verifier ever needs more heap, note it is a `JavaExec`, so use `tasks.verifyPlugin { maxHeapSize = ... }`. **Never `intellijPlatform.pluginVerification.freeArgs`** — those are appended to the verifier's own CLI arguments rather than the JVM's, which is why `0f11d0b` had to be reverted in `4f257bd`.

# Gradle properties applied ONLY on CI. Local builds never load this file, so
# nothing here affects `./gradlew` on a developer machine.
#
# .buildkite/pipeline.yml appends this file to $GRADLE_USER_HOME/gradle.properties,
# which Gradle reads natively and which takes precedence over the project's own
# gradle.properties.
#
# Why any of this is needed: the Buildkite hosted agents are 2 vCPU / 4 GB, and
# the docker plugin sets no memory limit on the container — so JVM ergonomics
# sizes heaps from whatever it detects rather than from the agent. Left alone,
# the Gradle daemon and the JVMs forked beside it together exceed the agent and
# the daemon is OOM-killed, which Gradle reports as the misleading
# "Gradle build daemon disappeared unexpectedly".

# Ceiling for the Gradle daemon. Deliberately below the project's 2048m so a
# forked test or verifier JVM still fits alongside it. This is a ceiling, not a
# reservation — steps that barely use the daemon do not pay for it.
org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx1536m -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=384m

# Compile inside the Gradle daemon rather than forking a separate ~2 GB Kotlin
# daemon. This is the single highest-leverage setting here.
kotlin.compiler.execution.strategy=in-process

# Ceiling for the forked test JVM. Read by the `test` block in build.gradle.kts;
# unset locally, where Gradle's default applies instead. There is no built-in
# gradle.properties key for a task's maxHeapSize, which is why that one line in
# the build script exists.
testMaxHeapSize=1g

task's maxHeapSize applied unconditionally, and the rest were scattered as -D
flags across pipeline steps.

$GRADLE_USER_HOME/gradle.properties, which Gradle reads natively and which
takes precedence over the project's gradle.properties — so nothing tracked in

One line stays in build.gradle.kts: a task's maxHeapSize has no equivalent
gradle.properties key, so `test` reads an optional testMaxHeapSize property.
It is unset locally, where Gradle's default applies.

- -PtestMaxHeapSize=1g passes

Done — build 64 green, and local config is untouched.

**How it's split now:**

- **`gradle/ci.properties`** — all CI memory tuning in one place: `org.gradle.jvmargs`, `kotlin.compiler.execution.strategy=in-process`, `testMaxHeapSize=1g`. Never loaded locally.
- **`.buildkite/pipeline.yml`** — appends that file to `$GRADLE_USER_HOME/gradle.properties`, which Gradle reads natively and which outranks the project's own `gradle.properties`. Shared between the Test and Verify steps via a YAML anchor, so the inline `-D` flags are gone.
- **`build.gradle.kts`** — one opt-in line: `providers.gradleProperty("testMaxHeapSize").orNull?.let { maxHeapSize = it }`.

That one line is unavoidable, and worth being explicit about: a task's `maxHeapSize` is a **task property**, and Gradle has no `gradle.properties` key for it. A properties file alone can't reach it. But since the property is unset locally, `./gradlew test` keeps Gradle's default heap — your local runs are genuinely unaffected.

**Verified rather than assumed:**
- `./gradlew test` with no property → passes (local unchanged)
- `-PtestMaxHeapSize=16m` → fails with `Initial heap size set to a larger value than the maximum heap size`, proving the property is actually applied rather than silently ignored
- CI log confirms all three properties landed on the agent

I also caught a real escaping bug while checking that log: Buildkite interpolates single-`$` variables at upload time, so `$GRADLE_USER_HOME` inside a *comment* rendered as empty on the agent. Behavior was fine — the executable code was escaped — but the comment was misleading. Fixed, and I swept the file for other unescaped variables (none).

**Two things to know before you merge:**

It reads `GITHUB_TOKEN` via `buildkite-agent secret get` (that secret exists) and installs `gh` into the Gradle image — both fixes for bugs I found, but neither has run for real. content.text:
Diagnosis is complete, and it's more interesting than a simple breakage.

## Why Qodana fails

`.idea/gradle.xml` pins the Gradle JVM to `jbr-17`, while the project has targeted 21 since the initial commit. **Both settings have been there since `b58bce4`, and main has the identical file** — so this is a long-standing latent misconfiguration, not something this branch introduced.

What makes it *surface* is Gradle model caching. When Qodana can reuse a cached project model it never resolves the JDK and passes. When something invalidates that model — a change to `build.gradle.kts` or `gradle.properties` — it performs a real import, tries to resolve `jbr-17`, fails to find it in a container shipping JBR 21.0.10, and throws.

The evidence lines up:

- Failures on this branch start at `dbda46f`, the first commit here to touch `build.gradle.kts`, and every run since has touched build files.
- April's failures (`3b86d09`, `6ae487c`, `0f11d0b`) were *also* all commits touching `build.gradle.kts` or `gradle.properties`.
- main passes because main rarely changes those files — its last run was `d7c29b6`, a source-only merge.

**The consequence you should care about:** this PR changes both `build.gradle.kts` and `gradle.properties`. So merging it will very likely turn Qodana red **on main**, for a bug that already existed there. Fixing it is worth doing as part of this PR rather than discovering it post-merge.

questions.question: How should I fix the Gradle JVM setting?

options.label: Set gradleJvm to #JAVA_HOME (Recommended)
options.description: Replace `jbr-17` with IntelliJ's #JAVA_HOME macro in .idea/gradle.xml. Resolves to whatever JDK the environment provides — JBR 21 in the Qodana container, your local JDK in the IDE — so it stops being pinned to a version the project abandoned. One-line change, fixes CI and local alike.

options.label: Remove the gradleJvm option
options.description: Delete the line and let IntelliJ pick a default. Same practical effect in CI, and arguably cleaner since the setting is machine-specific state that arguably should not be in version control at all. Slightly less explicit about intent.

options.label: Pin it to jbr-21
options.description: Match the container's JBR version directly. Most literal fix, but it re-pins to a specific runtime name and will break again the same way the next time the platform version moves.

options.label: Just diagnose, do not change it
options.description: Leave .idea/gradle.xml alone. Qodana keeps failing on this PR and will likely go red on main after merge — but the fix stays out of a CI-migration PR.
